title: Arma mutata. Culmen Priami
titleEn: Borrowed Arms and the Siege of Priam's Palace — Aeneid II.386–485
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Flushed with their first success, Coroebus proposes a trick: let them change shields and put on the Greeks' insignia, for who, against an enemy, asks whether it is cunning or courage? He himself puts on the plumed helmet and handsome shield of the dead Androgeos and belts on an Argive sword; Rhipeus, Dymas and all the young men gladly do the same, and, armed in fresh spoils, they go among the Greeks under no god of theirs, fight many a fight in the blind night and send many Danaans down to Orcus. Some of the Greeks run for the ships and the safe shore; some climb back in shameful terror into the horse's well-known belly. Aeneas breaks off to cry that no one may trust when the gods are unwilling: Cassandra, daughter of Priam, is being dragged by her loosened hair from Minerva's shrine, raising her blazing eyes to heaven in vain, since chains hold her hands. Coroebus cannot bear the sight and throws himself, a doomed man, into the column; the rest follow and charge in close order. Then their own side, taking them for Greeks from the temple roof, overwhelms them with missiles, and a piteous slaughter begins from the look of their arms and the mistake over the Greek crests. The Danaans, enraged by the loss of the maiden, gather from every side, Ajax, the two Atridae and the whole host of the Dolopes, like winds clashing when a whirlwind bursts, with Zephyr, Notus and Eurus, the woods hissing and Nereus stirring the sea from its depths. The Greeks routed earlier in the night reappear, see through the false shields and weapons, and mark their foreign speech. Overwhelmed by numbers, Coroebus is first to fall, at the altar of the warlike goddess, struck by Peneleus; Rhipeus, the justest of the Trojans, falls too (the gods thought otherwise); Hypanis and Dymas are killed by their own friends; and neither Panthus's piety nor Apollo's fillet protects him as he falls. Aeneas calls the ashes of Ilium to witness that he shunned no weapon nor chance of the Danaans and, had it been fated, earned his death by his own hand. Torn away from the rest, he goes with Iphitus (slowed by age) and Pelias (lame from Ulysses's wound), summoned by the shouting to Priam's palace. There the battle is greater than anywhere in the city: Mars unconquered, Greeks rushing at the roofs, a tortoise driven up at the threshold, ladders against the walls, the Greeks climbing with shields in the left hand and grasping the gables with the right; the Trojans tear down towers and roofs and roll down the gilded beams, the glory of their ancestors, while others guard the doors below with drawn swords. Aeneas and his men renew their courage to help the king's house. A hidden door and a passage between Priam's buildings, by which Andromache used to visit her parents-in-law and bring little Astyanax to his grandfather, let him climb to the roof, where the Trojans throw useless spears. They attack a tower at the brink with iron, wrench it from its seat and push it; it falls with a crash on the Greek ranks, but others come up and the missiles never cease. Before the forecourt Pyrrhus leaps, bright with bronze, like a snake fed on poison herbs that has shed its skin and rears to the sun; with him are Periphas, Automedon and the Scyrian youth, hurling fire at the roof. Pyrrhus himself seizes an axe, hews through the hard doors, tears the bronze-plated posts from their hinges and cuts through the oak to make a huge opening. The house lies open within, the long halls and the inner chambers of Priam and the kings of old, and armed men are seen standing on the inmost threshold.
part: Borrowed Arms and the Siege of Priam's Palace (II.386–485)

sentences.t:
Atque hic successu exsultans animisque Coroebus,
“O socii, qua prima inquit fortuna salutis
monstrat iter, quoque ostendit se dextra, sequamur
mutemus clipeos, Danaumque insignia nobis
aptemus: dolus an virtus, quis in hoste requirat?
sentences.l:
And here Coroebus, exulting in success and in spirit,
“O comrades, says he, where first fortune of safety
shows the road, and where she shows herself, favourable, let us follow;
let us change shields, and the Danaans' badges for ourselves
let us fit on: guile or courage, who in an enemy would ask?
sentences.i: Then Coroebus, exultant in his success and his courage, cried: “Friends, wherever fortune first points out the road to safety, and wherever she shows a kindly face, there let us follow; let us swap our shields and fit ourselves with the Greeks' badges. Craft or courage—who stops to ask, against a foe?
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'successu' and 'animis' are ablatives of cause with 'exsultans' ('exulting in'); the plural 'animis' is often 'courage, spirit'. The speech opens at 387 with the quotation mark Greenough prints, and 'inquit' sits inside it, as the verb of saying often does. 'qua… quoque' are relative adverbs, 'where… and where' (here 'quoque' is quo + que, not 'also'; the Latin Library's 'quaque' means the same). 'prima' agrees with 'fortuna' and is best rendered as an adverb, 'first'. 'dextra' is a feminine adjective, 'favourable', agreeing with the understood 'fortuna'. 'sequamur', 'mutemus' and 'aptemus' are first person plural jussive subjunctives, 'let us…', with no conjunctions between them (asyndeton). 'nobis' is a dative of the person for whom. 'Danaum' is the old genitive plural in -um (you'll see this constantly). 'dolus an virtus' sets two alternatives against each other, and 'requirat' is a potential subjunctive, 'who would ask?'.

sentences.t: Arma dabunt ipsi.
sentences.l: Arms they themselves will give.”
sentences.i: The Greeks themselves will furnish the arms.”
sentences.n: 'ipsi' is nominative plural, the Danaans themselves, subject of 'dabunt'. Greenough prints the closing speech mark after the full stop and before 'Sic', after a space; so the mark is carried in the `l` and `i` of this unit, where the speech ends, and heads the `t` of the next.

sentences.t:
”Sic fatus, deinde comantem
Androgei galeam clipeique insigne decorum
induitur, laterique Argivum accommodat ensem.
sentences.l:
Thus having spoken, then the crested
of Androgeos helmet and of the shield the handsome badge
he puts on, and to his side of the Argives fits the sword.
sentences.i: Having so spoken, he puts on the plumed helmet of Androgeos and the shield with its splendid device, and buckles an Argive sword to his side.
sentences.n: The closing speech mark ” heads this unit's `t` (see the previous note); it is not repeated in `l` or `i`. 'Sic fatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'for', 'having thus spoken' (you'll see this constantly). 'induitur' is passive in form but middle in sense and takes an accusative object, 'puts on (for himself)' ('galeam… insigne'). 'comantem' is a present participle used as an adjective, 'hairy, plumed', agreeing with 'galeam'. 'Androgei' is the genitive of the Greek name Androgeos, the Greek leader met in the previous part. 'laterique' is a dative with 'accommodat', 'fits to his side'. 'Argivum' is a genitive plural in -um, 'of the Argives'.

sentences.t:
Hoc Rhipeus, hoc ipse Dymas omnisque iuventus
laeta facit;
sentences.l:
This Rhipeus, this Dymas himself, and all the youth,
glad, does;
sentences.i: Rhipeus does the same, and Dymas himself, and all the young men, and gladly;
sentences.n: 'Hoc' is the object of 'facit', 'this' meaning changing arms. 'facit' is singular though the subjects are several; the verb agrees with the nearest, 'iuventus', a collective noun. 'laeta' agrees with the subject, 'gladly'. 'ipse' marks Dymas out by name.

sentences.t: spoliis se quisque recentibus armat.
sentences.l: with spoils, himself each one, fresh, arms.
sentences.i: each man arms himself in the spoils he has just won.
sentences.n: 'spoliis recentibus' is an ablative of means, 'with fresh spoils'. 'se… armat' is reflexive, 'arms himself'; 'quisque' ('each one') stands in the singular as the subject.

sentences.t:
Vadimus immixti Danais haud numine nostro,
multaque per caecam congressi proelia noctem
conserimus, multos Danaum demittimus Orco.
sentences.l:
We go, mingled with the Danaans, not with our own divinity,
and many battles through the blind night having met,
we join, many of the Danaans we send down to Orcus.
sentences.i: We go, mingled with the Greeks, and no god of ours goes with us; in the blind night we meet them and join many a fight, and send many of the Danaans down to Orcus.
sentences.n: The narration is in the first person: Aeneas is speaking. 'immixti' is a perfect passive participle with middle force, 'mingled with'. 'haud numine nostro' is an ablative, 'with a divinity not ours', that is, with the gods not on their side. 'congressi' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'congredior', 'having met'. 'proelia conserimus' is the idiom 'join battle'. 'caecam noctem' is the 'blind' night, in which nothing can be seen. 'Danaum' is the old genitive plural again. 'Orco' is a dative of direction with 'demittimus' (poetic); Orcus stands for the underworld.

sentences.t:
Diffugiunt alii ad navis, et litora cursu
fida petunt:
sentences.l:
Scatter some to the ships, and the shores in running
faithful they seek:
sentences.i: Some scatter in flight towards the ships, and run for the shore they can trust:
sentences.n: 'diffugiunt' (di-, 'in different directions') is the verb of scattering. 'navis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is for -es (you'll see this constantly). 'cursu' is an ablative of manner. 'fida' agrees with the neuter plural 'litora', 'trusty', the beach where the ships lie. The colon introduces the contrast with the next group.

sentences.t:
pars ingentem formidine turpi
scandunt rursus equum et nota conduntur in alvo.
sentences.l:
part, the huge horse, in shameful fear,
climb again, and in the known belly are hidden.
sentences.i: while others, in craven terror, scale the huge horse once more and hide themselves in the belly they know.
sentences.n: 'pars' is a singular collective noun with a plural verb ('scandunt'), as often. The adjective 'ingentem' is held apart from its noun 'equum' (next line) by 'formidine turpi'. 'formidine turpi' is an ablative of cause. 'conduntur' is passive in form with reflexive sense, 'are hidden, hide themselves'. 'nota… alvo' is the belly they had already occupied.

sentences.t: Heu nihil invitis fas quemquam fidere divis!
sentences.l: Alas, in nothing is it right anyone to trust, the gods unwilling!
sentences.i: Alas, it is not right for any man to trust, when the gods are unwilling!
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a cry from Aeneas looking back. 'fas' (with 'est' understood) is an indeclinable noun, 'what is right by divine law', and takes an infinitive: 'fidere' (a semi-deponent) with 'quemquam' as its accusative subject. 'nihil' is an adverbial accusative, 'in no way, not at all'. 'invitis divis' is an ablative absolute, 'the gods unwilling'. 'heu' is an exclamation of pain.

sentences.t:
Ecce trahebatur passis Priameïa virgo
crinibus a templo Cassandra adytisque Minervae,
ad caelum tendens ardentia lumina frustra,—
sentences.l:
Behold, was being dragged, with loosened, Priam's maiden,
locks, from the temple, Cassandra, and the shrines of Minerva,
to the sky stretching her blazing eyes, in vain,—
sentences.i: And see, the maiden daughter of Priam was being hauled by her loosened hair from the temple and shrine of Minerva—Cassandra— lifting her blazing eyes to heaven in vain—
sentences.n: 'trahebatur' is the imperfect passive, 'was being dragged', and 'Priameïa virgo' ('the Priamid maiden', adjective 'Priameïus' with Greenough's diaeresis) is its subject, with 'Cassandra' in apposition. 'passis crinibus' is an ablative of manner, 'with hair spread out', from 'pando'. 'a templo… adytisque' are ablatives of separation, 'from the temple and the inner shrines'. 'tendens' is a present participle, 'stretching'. 'ardentia' is 'blazing', of eyes. Cassandra is the Trojan prophetess whom no one would believe. The dash breaks off the sentence; the next unit picks up 'lumina'.

sentences.t: lumina, nam teneras arcebant vincula palmas.
sentences.l: eyes, for her tender palms chains were restraining.
sentences.i: her eyes, for chains held her tender hands fast.
sentences.n: 'lumina' is repeated from the line before, a resumptive repetition after the dash. 'nam' gives the reason why it is the eyes, not the hands, that she lifts. 'arcebant' is imperfect of 'arceo', 'hold off, confine'. 'palmas' is the accusative plural of 'palma', 'palm, hand'.

sentences.t:
Non tulit hanc speciem furiata mente Coroebus,
et sese medium iniecit periturus in agmen.
sentences.l:
Did not bear this sight, with maddened mind, Coroebus,
and himself, midway, he threw, about to die, into the column.
sentences.i: Coroebus could not endure the sight; with his mind aflame with fury he flung himself, a doomed man, into the very midst of their column.
sentences.n: 'furiata mente' is an ablative of manner, with 'furiata' a perfect passive participle (from 'furio', 'madden'), 'with maddened mind'. 'tulit' is the perfect of 'fero', here 'endured'. 'sese' is the emphatic form of 'se'. 'medium' is a predicate adjective, 'into the middle'. 'periturus' is the future participle of 'pereo', 'about to perish, doomed'; Virgil lets us see his fate in advance.

sentences.t: Consequimur cuncti et densis incurrimus armis.
sentences.l: We follow, all, and in dense arms we rush in.
sentences.i: We all follow, and charge in a close-packed mass of arms.
sentences.n: 'cuncti' is 'all together'. 'densis armis' is an ablative of manner, 'with close-packed arms', i.e. in close order. 'incurrimus' is 'we run in, charge'.

sentences.t:
Hic primum ex alto delubri culmine telis
nostrorum obruimur, oriturque miserrima caedes
armorum facie et Graiarum errore iubarum.
sentences.l:
Here first from the high summit of the shrine by the missiles
of our own men we are overwhelmed, and arises most pitiable slaughter
from the look of the arms and the error of the Greek crests.
sentences.i: Here first, from the high roof of the shrine, we are overwhelmed by the spears of our own countrymen, and a most piteous slaughter rises from the look of our armour and the blunder of the Greek crests.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'delubri' is the genitive of 'delubrum', 'shrine, temple'. 'ex alto… culmine' is an ablative of place from which; 'telis' is an ablative of means. 'nostrorum' is a genitive plural used as a noun, 'of our men'. 'obruimur' is passive, 'we are overwhelmed'. 'miserrima' is a superlative, 'most pitiable'. 'armorum facie' and 'errore' are ablatives of cause. 'Graiarum… iubarum' are feminine genitive plurals: 'iubae' are the crests, horsehair plumes, of helmets, which the disguised Trojans now wear.

sentences.i: Then the Greeks, stirred by the outcry and in rage at the maiden's rescue, gather from every side and fall upon us, fiercest Ajax and the two sons of Atreus, and the whole host of the Dolopes;
sentences.n: 'gemitu' and 'ira' are ablatives of cause; 'ereptae virginis' is a perfect passive participle, 'the maiden snatched away' (Cassandra, taken from them). 'collecti' is a perfect passive participle, 'gathered'. 'acerrimus' is the superlative of 'acer'. 'Atridae' are Agamemnon and Menelaus, the sons of Atreus. 'Dolopum' is a genitive plural in -um; the Dolopes were a people of Thessaly in the Greek army. The sentence is not finished by its punctuation: the semicolon introduces the simile.

sentences.i: Just as, at times, when a whirlwind has burst forth, the winds clash head-on, the west wind and the south, and Eurus, glad in his horses of the dawn;
sentences.n: A simile. 'ceu' is 'as'. 'adversi' is nominative plural, 'facing one another'. 'rupto turbine' is an ablative absolute, 'the whirlwind having burst'. 'quondam' is 'at times' in a simile. 'Zephyrus', 'Notus' and 'Eurus' are the west, south and east winds; 'Zephyrusque Notusque' is the double -que, 'both… and' (you'll see this constantly). 'Eois equis' is an ablative of cause or respect, 'in his eastern horses', the horses of the dawn.

sentences.t:
stridunt silvae, saevitque tridenti
spumeus atque imo Nereus ciet aequora fundo.
sentences.l:
hiss the woods, and rages with trident
foaming, and from the lowest bottom Nereus stirs the waters.
sentences.i: the woods shriek, and foam-flecked Nereus rages with his trident and churns up the sea from its lowest depths.
sentences.n: 'stridunt' is the verb for a hiss or shriek. 'tridenti' is an ablative of means, the sea-god's trident. 'spumeus' agrees with 'Nereus', a sea-god used here for the sea itself. 'imo… fundo' is an ablative of separation, 'from the lowest bottom'. 'ciet' is 'stirs up'; the whole simile compares the Greek onslaught to a storm on land and sea.

sentences.i: Those too, if any whom through the dark shadow of night we routed by an ambush and hunted over the whole city, now come into sight;
sentences.n: 'illi etiam' is 'those also', the Greeks scattered earlier. 'si quos' is 'if any', 'any whom'. 'fudimus' is the perfect of 'fundo', 'pour out, rout'. 'insidiis' is an ablative of means. 'apparent' is the present of 'appareo'; Greenough prints it with pp here and 'adp-' at 483–484 (the Latin Library prints pp throughout, with no difference of sense).

sentences.t:
primi clipeos mentitaque tela
adgnoscunt, atque ora sono discordia signant.
sentences.l:
first the shields and the lying weapons
they recognise, and the mouths, discordant in sound, they mark.
sentences.i: First of all they see through our shields and weapons that lie, and mark our speech, whose sound jars with their own.
sentences.n: 'primi' is nominative plural, agreeing with the subject and best rendered as an adverb, 'first'. 'mentita' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'mentior', here with passive sense, 'counterfeit'. 'adgnoscunt' is Greenough's spelling of 'agnoscunt' (you'll see this constantly: 'ad-' not assimilated). 'ora' is the neuter plural of 'os', 'mouths', hence 'speech', and 'discordia' agrees with it; 'sono' is an ablative of respect, 'in sound'. 'signant' is 'mark, take note of'.

sentences.t: Ilicet obruimur numero;
sentences.l: At once we are overwhelmed by number;
sentences.i: At once we are swamped by sheer numbers;
sentences.n: 'ilicet' is an adverb, 'at once' (it began as the formula 'ire licet', 'you may go'). 'numero' is an ablative of means, 'by numbers'.

sentences.i: And first Coroebus by Peneleus's right hand, at the war-goddess's altar, sinks to the ground;
sentences.n: 'primus' is the nominative, 'first'. 'Penelei' is the genitive of Peneleus, a Greek captain; 'dextra' is an ablative of means, 'by the right hand'. 'divae armipotentis' is the goddess 'mighty in arms', Minerva, whose temple has been the scene so far. 'ad aram' is 'at the altar'. 'procumbit' is 'falls forward, sinks down'.

sentences.t:
cadit et Rhipeus, iustissimus unus
qui fuit in Teucris et servantissimus aequi:
sentences.l:
falls also Rhipeus, most just, one man
who was among the Teucrians, and most observant of the right:
sentences.i: Rhipeus falls too, the one man most just of all the Trojans, and the most devoted to what is right:
sentences.n: 'cadit' is 'falls'. 'iustissimus unus' puts the superlative with 'unus' for emphasis, 'the one most just', pre-eminently so. 'Teucris' is an ablative with 'in', 'among the Teucrians', another name for the Trojans. 'servantissimus' is the superlative of the participle 'servans' used as an adjective, and takes the genitive 'aequi', 'most observant of the right'. The colon opens a comment on this death.

sentences.t: dis aliter visum;
sentences.l: to the gods otherwise it seemed;
sentences.i: The gods saw it another way;
sentences.n: 'visum' is the participle with 'est' understood, 'it seemed (good)'. 'dis' is a dative, 'to the gods', the persons for whom it seemed so. The comment is brief, with no explanation, as the poem leaves it.

sentences.t:
pereunt Hypanisque Dymasque
confixi a sociis;
sentences.l:
perish both Hypanis and Dymas
pierced through by comrades;
sentences.i: Hypanis and Dymas perish too, run through by their own friends;
sentences.n: 'pereunt' is plural for the two subjects. 'Hypanisque Dymasque' is the double -que, 'both… and'. 'confixi' is a perfect passive participle of 'configo', 'pierced through'. 'a sociis' is the agent, 'by comrades': the Trojans on the roof, mistaking them for Greeks.

sentences.t:
nec te tua plurima, Panthu,
labentem pietas nec Apollinis infula texit.
sentences.l:
nor you, your very great, Panthus,
falling, piety nor of Apollo the fillet covered.
sentences.i: nor did your abundant piety, Panthus, nor Apollo's fillet, shield you as you fell.
sentences.n: 'te… Panthu' is an address (apostrophe) to Panthus, the priest of Apollo from the previous part. 'tua plurima… pietas' is split by 'Panthu, labentem' (hyperbaton); 'plurima' is the superlative of 'multus', 'very great'. 'labentem' is a present participle, 'as you fell, slipping'. 'nec… nec' is 'neither… nor'. 'infula' is the woollen fillet worn by priests. 'texit' is the perfect, 'covered, protected'.

sentences.t:
Iliaci cineres et flamma extrema meorum,
testor, in occasu vestro nec tela nec ullas
vitavisse vices Danaum, et, si fata fuissent
ut caderem, meruisse manu.
sentences.l:
Ashes of Ilium, and last flame of my own,
I call to witness, at your fall neither weapons nor any
to have avoided, the turns of the Danaans, and, if the fates had been
that I should fall, to have deserved it by hand.
sentences.i: Ashes of Ilium, last flames of my own people, I call you to witness: at your fall I shunned neither weapons nor any of the Danaans' onsets, and, had the fates decreed that I should fall, I earned it by my own hand.
sentences.n: The narrator turns to address the burning city: 'cineres' and 'flamma' are vocatives, identical in form to the nominative. 'meorum' is a genitive plural used as a noun, 'of my people'. 'testor' is a deponent, 'I call to witness', followed by the infinitives 'vitavisse' and 'meruisse' in indirect statement, with the subject 'me' left out. 'in occasu vestro' is 'at your setting', that is, your fall ('occasus' is the setting of a heavenly body). 'nec tela nec ullas… vices' is 'neither weapons nor any… turns', 'vices' meaning the chances or onsets of the Danaans; 'Danaum' is the genitive plural in -um. 'si fata fuissent ut caderem' is 'if the fates had been (such) that I should fall', with a clause of result; 'meruisse manu' is the perfect infinitive, 'to have earned it'.

sentences.i: We are wrenched away from that place, Iphitus and Pelias with me, Iphitus now weighed down by years, and Pelias slowed by a wound that Ulysses gave;
sentences.n: 'divellimur' is passive, 'we are torn apart (from the rest)'. 'quorum' is a relative pronoun, 'of whom', with 'Iphitus… Pelias' distributing the two. 'aevo' is an ablative of cause, 'by age'; 'gravior' is comparative, 'rather heavy, weighed down'. 'volnere' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnere'. 'tardus' is 'slow'. 'Ulixi' is the genitive of 'Ulixes' in -i.

sentences.t: protinus ad sedes Priami clamore vocati.
sentences.l: straightaway to the seat of Priam by the shout called.
sentences.i: straight to Priam's palace, summoned by the clamour.
sentences.n: 'vocati' is a perfect passive participle, masculine plural, agreeing with the 'we' of the sentence, 'summoned'. 'clamore' is an ablative of means. 'sedes' (plural) is 'abode', here Priam's palace.

sentences.t:
Hic vero ingentem pugnam, ceu cetera nusquam
bella forent, nulli tota morerentur in urbe.
sentences.l:
Here indeed a huge fight, as if the rest
wars were nowhere, none were dying in the whole city.
sentences.i: Here, truly, a battle so vast—as if there were no other fighting anywhere, as if no one were dying in all the city.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'pugnam' is the object of 'cernimus' in 441, held back two lines for effect. 'Hic vero' is 'here indeed', marking the climax. 'ceu… forent… morerentur' are imperfect subjunctives in a comparison 'as if'; 'forent' is a form of 'essent'. 'cetera… bella' is 'the other wars', and 'nusquam' 'nowhere'. 'nulli' is nominative plural, 'none'.

sentences.t:
Sic Martem indomitum, Danaosque ad tecta ruentis
cernimus, obsessumque acta testudine limen.
sentences.l:
Thus Mars unconquered, and the Danaans to the roofs rushing,
we see, and besieged, a tortoise having been driven, the threshold.
sentences.i: So we behold the god of war unconquered, and the Greeks rushing at the roofs, and the threshold besieged beneath a tortoise driven up to it.
sentences.n: 'Sic' resumes the 'ceu' scene of the previous unit and leads into the verb 'cernimus'. 'Martem' is the god of war put for war itself. 'indomitum' is 'unconquered'. 'ruentis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is, a present participle. 'obsessum… limen' is a perfect passive participle with 'limen', 'the threshold besieged'. 'acta testudine' is an ablative absolute: the 'testudo' ('tortoise') is a covering of locked shields, or a movable shed, driven forward against the door.

sentences.t:
Haerent parietibus scalae, postisque sub ipsos
nituntur gradibus, clipeosque ad tela sinistris
protecti obiciunt, prensant fastigia dextris.
sentences.l:
Cling to the walls the ladders, and beneath the very doorposts
they strain on steps, and shields toward missiles with left hands
covered they hold out, they grasp the gables with right hands.
sentences.i: Ladders cling to the walls, and right under the doorposts they strain up the rungs, and, covered, hold their shields out against the missiles with the left hand, and with the right grasp the gables.
sentences.n: 'parietibus' is a dative with 'haerent'. 'postis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is. 'gradibus' is an ablative of means, 'by the steps' (the rungs). 'nituntur' is a deponent, 'strain, climb'. 'protecti' is a perfect passive participle, 'covered', agreeing with the climbers. 'sinistris… dextris' are ablatives of means with 'manibus' understood. 'fastigia' are the gable-tops or roof-edges. 'prensant' is a frequentative of 'prehendo', 'keep grasping'.

sentences.t:
Dardanidae contra turris ac tota domorum
culmina convellunt;
sentences.l:
The Dardanids, in return, towers and all the houses'
roofs tear up;
sentences.i: The Dardanians, for their part, tear down the towers and the whole roofs of their houses;
sentences.n: 'Dardanidae' is the nominative plural of the patronymic, 'descendants of Dardanus', the Trojans. 'contra' is an adverb, 'in return'. 'turris' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is for -es. 'domorum' is the genitive plural of 'domus'. 'convellunt' is 'tear up, tear loose'; the roofs and towers become missiles.

sentences.t:
his se, quando ultima cernunt,
extrema iam in morte parant defendere telis;
sentences.l:
with these, themselves, since the last things they see,
in extreme now at death they prepare to defend with weapons;
sentences.i: With these, since they see the end is come, they make ready to defend themselves at death's last edge, and make them their weapons;
sentences.n: 'his… telis' is 'with these as weapons', the ablative of means with 'telis' in the predicate sense. 'quando' is causal, 'since'. 'ultima cernunt' is 'see the last things' (the end). 'parant defendere' is 'prepare to defend', with 'se' as the object. 'extrema in morte' is 'at the very edge of death'.

sentences.t:
auratasque trabes, veterum decora alta parentum,
devolvunt;
sentences.l:
and gilded beams, the lofty glories of ancient forefathers,
they roll down;
sentences.i: The gilded rafters too, the high glory of their fathers of old, they send rolling down;
sentences.n: '-que' joins this clause to the last; 'trabes' is the object of 'devolvunt'. 'decora alta' is an apposition, 'lofty ornaments', the neuter plural of 'decus'. 'veterum… parentum' are genitive plurals, 'of ancient forefathers'. 'devolvunt' is 'roll down'.

sentences.t:
alii strictis mucronibus imas
obsedere fores;
sentences.l:
others with drawn sword-points the lowest
have beset the doors;
sentences.i: while others, swords drawn, have taken up their post at the doors below;
sentences.n: 'strictis mucronibus' is an ablative absolute or ablative of manner, 'with drawn blades'. 'obsedere' is 'obsederunt', the perfect with -ere for -erunt (you'll see this constantly). 'imas fores' are the doors at the bottom, the lowest entrances.

sentences.t: has servant agmine denso.
sentences.l: these they guard in a dense column.
sentences.i: these they hold in a close-packed line.
sentences.n: 'has' refers to 'imas fores'. 'servant' is 'guard'. 'agmine denso' is an ablative of manner, 'in a dense line'.

sentences.t:
Instaurati animi, regis succurrere tectis,
auxilioque levare viros, vimque addere victis.
sentences.l:
Renewed are our spirits, to the king's roofs to bring help,
and with aid to relieve the men, and add force to the conquered.
sentences.i: Our courage is renewed: to bring help to the king's house, to relieve its defenders with our aid, and lend strength to the beaten.
sentences.n: 'instaurati animi' leaves out the verb 'sunt', 'spirits are renewed'. 'succurrere', 'levare' and 'addere' are infinitives of purpose, 'to help… to relieve… to add', a poetic use. 'tectis' is a dative with 'succurrere'. 'auxilio' is an ablative of means. 'viros' are the defenders. 'victis' is a dative, 'to the conquered'.

sentences.t:
Limen erat caecaeque fores et pervius usus
tectorum inter se Priami, postesque relicti
a tergo, infelix qua se, dum regna manebant,
saepius Andromache ferre incomitata solebat
ad soceros, et avo puerum Astyanacta trahebat.
sentences.l:
A threshold there was, and blind doors, and a passable use
of the buildings of Priam among each other, and posts left
behind, by which unhappy, while the kingdom stood,
more often Andromache, unaccompanied, used to bear herself
to her parents-in-law, and to his grandfather the boy Astyanax drew.
sentences.i: There was a threshold, and a hidden door, and a way through linking Priam's buildings one with another, and back doors left at the rear, by which unhappy Andromache, while the kingdom stood, would often go, unattended, to her husband's parents, leading the boy Astyanax to his grandfather.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Limen erat' is 'there was a threshold'. 'caecae fores' are 'blind doors', that is hidden ones. 'pervius usus' is a passage that can be used. 'tectorum inter se' is 'of the buildings among themselves', in the sense 'between one another'. 'postes relicti a tergo' are back doors. 'qua' is a relative adverb, 'by which'. 'infelix' is a foreshadowing epithet. 'saepius' is comparative, 'rather often'. 'solebat' takes the infinitive 'ferre', and 'se ferre' is 'to betake herself'. 'soceros' are her parents-in-law (Hector's parents). 'avo' is a dative, 'to the grandfather'. 'Astyanacta' is the Greek accusative of Astyanax, Hector's small son. 'dum regna manebant' is 'while the kingdom stood' (imperfect indicative).

sentences.t:
Evado ad summi fastigia culminis, unde
tela manu miseri iactabant inrita Teucri.
sentences.l:
I come out to the summit of the highest roof, whence
weapons by hand the wretched Teucrians were hurling, useless.
sentences.i: I make my way up to the topmost gable of the roof, from where the luckless Trojans were hurling their weapons to no effect.
sentences.n: 'evado' is 'climb out, make my way up'. 'summi culminis' is the genitive, 'of the highest roof'. 'unde' is a relative adverb, 'from where'. 'manu' is an ablative of means, 'by hand'. 'inrita' is Greenough's spelling (the usual 'irrita'), 'useless', agreeing with 'tela'. 'miseri' is 'wretched, unlucky'. The imperfect 'iactabant' shows what was going on.

sentences.t:
Turrim in praecipiti stantem summisque sub astra
eductam tectis, unde omnis Troia videri
et Danaum solitae naves et Achaia castra,
sentences.l:
The tower, on a steep edge standing, and with topmost
roofs raised up under the stars, whence all Troy to be seen
and the Danaans' ships and the Achaean camp were wont,
sentences.i: The tower that stood at the very brink and rose with its topmost roofs toward the stars, from which all Troy used to be seen, with the Danaans' ships and the Achaean camp,
sentences.n: 'Turrim' is the object of 'convellimus', held to 464, with a comma and a long descriptive clause between. 'in praecipiti' is 'on the steep edge'. 'summis… tectis' is an ablative of description, 'with its topmost roofs'. 'sub astra' is 'up toward the stars'. 'unde… videri solitae' is 'from which were wont to be seen'; the participle 'solitae' agrees with the nearest subject 'naves' and serves for all the subjects. 'Danaum' is again the genitive plural in -um. 'Achaia' is a neuter plural adjective, 'Achaean'; the Latin Library has 'Achaica', which means the same.

sentences.i: we set on it with iron all round, where the upper storeys showed joints that were working loose, and wrench it from its high seat, and push it over;
sentences.n: 'adgressi' is a perfect participle of the deponent 'adgredior' (Greenough's spelling of 'aggredior'), 'having attacked'. 'ferro' is an ablative of means, 'iron' for tools. 'circum' is an adverb, 'all round'. 'qua' is 'where'. 'tabulata' are the floors or storeys of the tower. 'labantis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is, from the present participle 'labans', agreeing with 'iuncturas', 'loosening joints'. 'altis sedibus' is an ablative of separation, 'from its high seat'. 'impulimus' is the perfect.

sentences.t:
ea lapsa repente ruinam
cum sonitu trahit et Danaum super agmina late
incidit:
sentences.l:
it, having slipped, suddenly a ruin
with a crash drags and over the Danaans' ranks widely
falls:
sentences.i: It slips, and suddenly brings ruin down with a crash, and far and wide over the Danaan ranks it falls:
sentences.n: 'ea' (fem.) picks up the accusative 'turrim' and becomes the subject of the new clause. 'lapsa' is a perfect participle of the deponent 'labor', 'having slipped'. 'ruinam trahit' is an idiom, 'drags ruin with it, falls in ruin'. 'cum sonitu' is 'with a crash'. 'Danaum super agmina' puts the preposition 'super' between genitive and noun.

sentences.t:
ast alii subeunt, nec saxa, nec ullum
telorum interea cessat genus.
sentences.l:
but others come up, neither stones, nor any
of weapons meanwhile ceases kind.
sentences.i: but others come on in their place, and neither stones nor any kind of missile meanwhile lets up.
sentences.n: 'ast' is a poetic form of 'at', 'but'. 'subeunt' is 'come up, step in'. 'nec saxa, nec ullum… genus' is a double 'nec', with the verb 'cessat' singular, agreeing with the nearest subject, 'genus'. This is a half-line: Virgil left the verse unfinished, and Greenough prints it short. The paragraph ends here.

sentences.t:
Vestibulum ante ipsum primoque in limine Pyrrhus
exsultat, telis et luce coruscus aëna;
sentences.l:
Before the very forecourt and on the first threshold Pyrrhus
exults, with weapons and with brazen light gleaming;
sentences.i: In the very forecourt, on the first threshold, Pyrrhus leaps in triumph, flashing with weapons and the gleam of bronze;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. Pyrrhus (also called Neoptolemus) is the son of Achilles. 'Vestibulum ante ipsum' puts the preposition after its noun. 'exsultat' is 'leaps, exults'. 'coruscus' is 'flashing', with 'telis et luce… aëna' as ablatives of means; 'aëna' (Greenough's diaeresis, three syllables) is 'brazen', the Latin Library's 'aena'.

sentences.t:
qualis ubi in lucem coluber mala gramina pastus
frigida sub terra tumidum quem bruma tegebat,
nunc, positis novus exuviis nitidusque iuventa,
lubrica convolvit sublato pectore terga
arduus ad solem, et linguis micat ore trisulcis.
sentences.l:
such as when into the light a snake, evil herbs having fed on,
which cold under the earth winter, swollen, had covered,
now, laid aside the cast skins, new and glossy with youth,
rolls its slippery back, the breast lifted,
lofty to the sun, and with tongues flickers from the mouth three-forked.
sentences.i: Like a snake that comes out into the light, fed on poisonous herbs, swollen, that winter hid beneath the chill earth; now, its slough laid aside, fresh and gleaming with youth, it coils its slippery back and lifts its breast, rearing to the sun, three-forked tongues flickering at its mouth.
sentences.n: A simile: 'qualis ubi' is 'such as when', Pyrrhus is the snake, and the snake's verbs are 'convolvit' and 'micat'. 'pastus' is the perfect participle of 'pascor' (passive of 'pasco' with middle sense), 'having fed on', with the accusative 'mala gramina' (an object accusative, as with a transitive verb). 'quem' is a relative, with 'coluber' as its antecedent; 'tumidum' agrees with it, 'swollen'. 'bruma' is winter. 'positis exuviis' and 'sublato pectore' are ablatives absolute. 'iuventa' is an ablative of respect, 'in youth'. 'arduus' is 'towering'. 'linguis… trisulcis' is an ablative of means with 'ore' an ablative of place.

sentences.t:
Una ingens Periphas et equorum agitator Achillis,
armiger Automedon, una omnis Scyria pubes
succedunt tecto, et flammas ad culmina iactant.
sentences.l:
Together huge Periphas and the driver of Achilles's horses,
armour-bearer Automedon, together all the Scyrian youth
approach the roof, and flames to the summits hurl.
sentences.i: With him come huge Periphas, and the driver of Achilles's horses, his armour-bearer Automedon, and with them all the young men of Scyros, who press up to the roof and hurl flames at its summits.
sentences.n: 'una… una' is the adverb 'together', repeated. 'et' joins Periphas and Automedon, and 'equorum agitator Achillis' and 'armiger' are both in apposition to Automedon. 'Achillis' is the genitive of the Greek name. 'Scyria pubes' is a collective, 'the youth of Scyros', the island in the Aegean; the verb 'succedunt' is plural because several subjects are named. 'succedunt tecto' is a dative, 'draw up to the roof'. 'ad culmina' is 'at the summits'.

sentences.i: He himself, in the first rank, seizes a two-edged axe and hews through the stubborn doors, and wrenches their posts clear of the hinge, bronze-plated as they are;
sentences.n: 'ipse' is Pyrrhus. 'correpta… bipenni' is an ablative absolute, 'the double-edged axe having been seized'. 'dura limina' means the hard thresholds, that is the doors. 'perrumpit' is 'breaks right through'. 'postis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is; 'a cardine' is 'from the hinge'. 'aeratos' is 'bronze-clad'.

sentences.t:
iamque excisa trabe firma cavavit
robora, et ingentem lato dedit ore fenestram.
sentences.l:
and now, a beam cut out, the firm hollowed
oak-timbers, and a huge window gave with a wide mouth.
sentences.i: and now, with a beam hewn out, he has hollowed the sturdy oak, and made a huge opening, wide-mouthed.
sentences.n: 'excisa trabe' is an ablative absolute, 'a beam cut out'. 'cavavit' is the perfect of 'cavo', 'hollow'. 'firma… robora' are 'the firm oak-timbers'. 'lato… ore' is an ablative of manner, 'with a wide mouth'. 'fenestram' is here a window-like gap, the breach.

sentences.t: Adparet domus intus, et atria longa patescunt;
sentences.l: Appears the house within, and the halls long lie open;
sentences.i: The house comes into view within, and the long halls lie open;
sentences.n: 'Adparet' is Greenough's spelling of 'apparet' (you'll see this constantly: 'ad-' not assimilated; the Latin Library has 'apparet', with the same sense). 'domus' is nominative. 'atria' is the neuter plural of 'atrium'. 'patescunt' is the inchoative of 'pateo', 'lie open, stand revealed'.

sentences.t:
adparent Priami et veterum penetralia regum,
armatosque vident stantis in limine primo.
sentences.l:
appear the inmost parts of Priam and of ancient kings,
and armed men they see standing on the first threshold.
sentences.i: the inner chambers of Priam and of the kings of old stand exposed, and they see armed men standing at the first threshold.
sentences.n: 'adparent' is a plural verb for the neuter plural 'penetralia', 'the innermost parts'. 'veterum… regum' is 'of ancient kings'. The subject of 'vident' is the attackers, 'they'. 'armatos' is 'armed men', and 'stantis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is, present participle. 'in limine primo' is 'at the first threshold'.
